title: Divyanshi Choudhary Breaks Down After Last-Minute Asian Games Wushu Axing
excerpt: The 18-year-old wushu player beat Roshibina Devi in the selection trials and had already collected her India kit for Aichi-Nagoya — then was dropped days before departure, citing a knee injury her camp calls treatable.
body:
• Wushu athlete Divyanshi Choudhary, 18, was dropped from India's Asian Games 2026 squad in the women's 60kg Sanda category days before departure for Aichi-Nagoya.
  • Choudhary says she defeated replacement Roshibina Devi in the June selection trials and calls her removal an abuse of power; the federation says an MRI revealed a partial high-grade ACL tear.
  • Her family and coach say the injury was treatable with rehabilitation and challenge a decision delivered without written reasons.

Divyanshi Choudhary had collected her India kit, secured her flight tickets and stood with the national contingent at the Indian Olympic Association's send-off ceremony in New Delhi. On Friday morning, the 18-year-old wushu athlete recorded a nearly nine-minute video in tears from the roof of her hostel at the National Institute of Sports in Patiala: she had been axed from the Asian Games 2026 squad.

"I'm tired of this... I have been mentally harassed so much," she said in the video, which spread rapidly on September 11. "Since June, July, they have been after me because she (Roshibina) wanted to go. Given that I beat her, why is it a problem for her now? I beat her, it's my right to go there (Japan). She has been knocking at different doors... it's abuse of power." Choudhary said she was removed from the women's 60kg category and replaced by Naorem Roshibina Devi, whom she had beaten in the trials. She also said she no longer saw a reason to keep living — a statement that triggered widespread concern for her wellbeing.

Context & Background

Choudhary, from Kota, Rajasthan, won the trials in Srinagar (June 5–8) and reported to the preparatory camp at NIS Patiala on August 10.

The Wushu Association of India, in a statement by secretary Vijay Saraf, says Choudhary complained of hamstring pain in mid-August and stopped training altogether on August 21, when a physio found knee swelling. An MRI on August 23 at Manipal Hospital revealed a partial high-grade ACL tear with large effusion; doctors advised against competitive training and recommended surgery. WAI president Jitender Bajwa said the Sports Authority of India took the decision, not the federation, and CEO Suhel Ahmed added: "going by the rules, we can't send injured players."

Bajwa explained the replacement choice: Himanshi of Chandigarh, the losing finalist in the trials, suffered a jaw fracture and was unavailable, so coaches recommended Roshibina Devi — a world medallist and Arjuna awardee — as the standby.

"I beat her, it's my right to go there."

— Divyanshi Choudhary

The athlete's camp disputes this. Her father, Sunil, said the family was informed only on Friday morning with no reason given, and alleged the plan was to tell Divyanshi only at the airport. He confirmed the knee injury but said doctors advised it could be treated with rehabilitation. Her coach, Ashok Gautam, said she was the top performer across five selection trials over the past year and that proper taping would have been enough.

Impact & Analysis

The dispute pits two versions against each other: a medical unfitness call by SAI doctors days before departure, versus a trial-winning teenager who says she was cleared to compete and was pushed aside to accommodate a senior, decorated athlete. Neither side has published the medical reports or a written selection order, and the claim that no reasons were given in writing leaves the decision open to exactly the suspicion Choudhary voiced.

It also spotlights how grievances surface in Indian Olympic sports — through an anguished video from a hostel roof, not a formal appeals process. India's wushu programme has genuine medal contenders: Roshibina won silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Games in the same 60kg category. But the row has overshadowed the contingent's final preparations and renewed questions about federation transparency, where the gap between "medically unfit" and "fit with taping" becomes a verdict on an athlete's career.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian-origin fans in the US, UK and Canada, the Asian Games are one of the rare stages where India's Olympic sports beyond cricket command a global audience, and wushu has quietly become a medal prospect. This controversy is the kind of governance failure diaspora sports fans follow with frustration: a system that produces world-class athletes but cannot give a trial winner a clear, timely, written answer about why she was dropped.

What's Next

The contingent heads to Aichi-Nagoya with Roshibina Devi named in the women's 60kg Sanda category. The Wushu Association of India has announced no review of the selection process and no formal appeal channel for Choudhary. The immediate concern raised by her video is her wellbeing — and whether the system has any mechanism for an athlete in distress to be heard before she must plead her case to a camera. Anyone in emotional distress can reach India's 24x7 Tele MANAS helpline at 14416.
